title: Chapter 44: Sterling's Gift, Part 1 of 5: The Waiting
html:
The bells of the city came down the river one at a time, and Lyra counted them.
She sat on her upturned bucket by the brazier in the first arch, with her back to the brick and her knees drawn up, and the Ledger held flat against her chest under her coat, and Remy Castellan's little black book on her lap. The brazier had burned down to a red heap. Every so often a coal fell in on itself with a soft sound, like a sigh, and a few sparks went up into the dark and went out before they reached the roof.
The arch was a long low tunnel of old black brick, curved overhead like the inside of a barrel, and it ran back into the bank of the river further than the light went. The brick sweated. It always sweated. Little drops stood on it and ran down in the cold, and froze in thin gray beards along the bottom where the wall met the floor. The floor was beaten earth, hard as stone, strewn with straw and old sacking. Somewhere further in, past the second brazier, somebody was snoring. Somebody else was coughing, a long dry cough that went on and on and then stopped. A baby made a small sound, and a woman said hush, hush in a voice that was nearly asleep itself.
Forty-one people lived in the arches. Lyra had counted them too, on her first night, without meaning to. It was a thing she did now. She counted things. Steps. Bells. People. Her mother's memories. She had five, once. Now she had four. She counted them, too, sometimes, in the dark, the way you count coins in your pocket to make sure none have fallen through a hole.
The brushing. One hundred strokes, counted in a language she did not speak.
The rain on Crown Walk, and her father's voice: Isolde, you'll catch your death.
The empty chair at Midwinter.
The song that went up and hung.
That was four. The fifth, the cloak and the gray gloves and the carriage in the front hall, she had given to the Duke of Marrow on Saturday, in a gallery of black glass. She could feel the place where it had been. It was not like a hole. It was more like a step that was not there, in the dark, when you put your foot down for it.
The bell of Saint Bride's, up the hill, finished striking eleven.
Lyra did not move.
They had gone at the ninth bell. Corin and Gideon and Remy. Out of the mouth of the arch and up the frozen Steps into the dark, a lame old lamp boy with a squint, and a boy with his arm in a sling, and a young man in a gray coat with his hat in his hand. She had not come to the mouth of the arch to watch them go. She had told herself it was because the cold came in at the mouth, and she had a cough starting, and the Ledger must not get damp. That was not why.
She opened Remy's black book again, by the red light of the coals, and turned the pages without reading them.
What the Lady took. Kept by R. C., from the year he was ten.
She did not need to read it. She had read it all afternoon and all evening, page after page, in the small careful hand. Names, and dates, and what was taken, and who it was sold to, and the last column, the one Remy had added himself, the one with nothing printed at the top but the word he had written there in pencil. AFTER. She had read that column most of all. Went home. Did not know his wife. Sat down in the street. Hanged himself, the Tuesday. Did not know.
And near the back, the line that was crossed out, with a small flower drawn over the crossing. Tam's line.
She closed the book.
Across the arch, on the far side of the brazier, Mother Grue was packing.
She had been packing since the eighth bell. Slowly, the way she did everything, leaning on her stick, in her heap of shawls, with her beak of a nose catching the red light. She did not pack her own things. She did not seem to have any. She packed the arches. A tin pot, a pile of blankets, a bag of meal, a coil of rope. Each thing she picked up, she looked at for a moment, the way you look at a face, and then put it in one of the sacks at her feet, or put it back where it had been. The sacks were for tomorrow. For the rope-walk. For Lascar Mary's fire on the Saltmarsh, where forty-one people were going to walk in the dark before the dawn, because a man called Gant was coming at first light with six men and a warrant.
"You'll wear the floor through, girl," said Mother Grue, without looking up.
"I'm not moving."
"Your eyes are." Mother Grue put a tin cup in a sack. "Up the Steps and down again. Up and down. Like a dog waiting at a door." She picked up a wooden spoon and looked at it. "He'll come or he won't. Watching the Steps won't bring him faster."
Lyra looked down at her hands. They were red with cold, and rough, and there was ink in the cracks of the knuckles from the Ledger. Two weeks ago they had been soft. Two weeks ago they had worn gloves of white kid that came up past the wrist, and she had not known that the skin on the back of your hands could split in the cold like the bark of a tree.
"If he isn't back by the first bell after midnight," she said, "Oren will go in."
"I know."
"And if Oren goes in, and doesn't come back—"
"Then you'll take that book," said Mother Grue, "and the other one, and you'll go up the hill to Saint Bride's with the doctor, as you said you would, and you won't look back. As you said you would." She put the spoon in the sack. "Isn't that the plan?"
"That's the plan."
"Then stop chewing on it. You'll break a tooth."
The coals sighed in the brazier.
Out beyond the mouth of the arch, the river went by in the dark. Lyra could hear it, under everything. Not loud. The river was half ice now, at the edges, and the ice ground and creaked against itself as the black water pushed it along, a long low grinding like a mill a long way off. Every so often there was a crack, sharp as a shot, when a sheet of it broke against a pier of the bridge downstream. The first time she had heard that, on the barge, she had thought it was a gun.
Now she only counted them.
At half past eleven, the canvas over the mouth of the arch moved.
Lyra was on her feet before she knew it. The Ledger was in her hand. Remy's book had fallen into the straw.
It was Oren.
He came in stooping, under the low brick, with the snow on his shoulders and on the brim of his hat, and the cold came in with him like a dog. He was in Terrence's coat, the long brown one with the patched elbows that Marta had given him, and it was too short in the arms for him, so that his big wrists stuck out, red and raw. His face was gray with cold. His beard had ice in it.
He looked at Lyra standing there with the Ledger in her hand. He looked past her, into the arch, at the empty pallet by the wall where Corin had been lying all afternoon with his leg bound from hip to ankle.
He did not ask. He saw it.
"Not yet," said Lyra.
Oren nodded, once, slowly. He came to the brazier and held his hands over it. They were shaking. Not from fear. From cold. He had walked from the Bridewell, across the whole of the Lower Docks, in the snow, in a coat that was too short in the arms.
"Ellis?" said Lyra.
"Came." Oren's voice was rough, as if he had not used it all day. "Waited in the stable with the horses. He had the note." He put his hand inside Terrence's coat and took out a small square of paper, folded in four, and held it up for her to see, and put it back. "The one I sent for Moll, by him. She came to the barge herself before he could give it her. No sense leaving it in a carter's coat for a constable to find." He held his hands over the coals again. "I told him what to tell Hessa. By mouth. Nothing on paper. He'll be at Withy Reach by tomorrow night."
"What did you tell him?"
"Go further than hay goes." Oren looked at the coals. "She'll know."
Lyra sat down again on her bucket. Slowly. She bent and picked Remy's book up out of the straw and brushed it off and held it on her knee.
"And Juno?" she said.
"Ellis says the barge is still at the barn. Under the broken roof. Your father's sleeping. Tapping, still, when he's awake." Oren paused. "And Juno asked for you. Every day. Ellis says she's mending. Her feet. She can stand now." He paused again. "She has your letter still. To your brother. In her coat. She won't let go of it."
Lyra did not say anything.
She had written that letter on the barge, nearly a week ago, on the back of a page torn out of Hessa's ledger. Ro. It's me. I'm alive. Father's alive. I can explain everything, if you'll let me. Meet me. Anywhere. Alone. L. And folded it in three, the way you fold a letter, not small, not clever, and given it to a girl of fourteen with frostbitten feet, because there was nobody else to give it to.
She did not know if Rowan would read it. She did not know if he would burn it, or give it to Kross, or put it in his pocket and carry it unread for the rest of his life. She did not know anything about her brother any more. Only that he was sixteen, and wore a cadet's gray coat, and folded his sweet wrappers small, the way Silas Kross had taught him. And that he thought she had ruined the family.
"Ellis will bring her," said Oren. "If she can walk. Thursday, maybe. On the straw wain. Hessa can put her ashore at Withy Reach." He looked at Lyra. "If you want."
"I want."
Oren nodded.
The bell of Saint Bride's struck the quarter.
Then it struck the half.
Then, a long, long time later, it began to strike midnight, and Lyra counted every stroke, and on the twelfth, Oren took his hands away from the coals and stood up straight, as straight as the low brick roof would let him, and buttoned Terrence's coat to the throat.
He did not say anything.
He went to the wall where Corin's things were, and took down the short iron bar that Mother Grue's people used for breaking the ice on the water butts, and weighed it in his hand.
"One more bell," said Lyra. "You said the first bell after midnight. Not midnight."
Oren stood with the iron bar in his hand, and looked at her.
"One more bell," he said.
And he sat down again, on the floor this time, with his back to the wall and the iron bar across his knees, facing the canvas over the mouth of the arch, and waited.
The Coal Store
They heard him before they saw him.
Not his voice. His leg. A dragging sound on the frozen Steps outside, slow and heavy, like a sack being pulled down stone. Then a stop. Then the drag again. And under it, very low, somebody humming. A tune that went down at the end like a man setting a heavy box on the ground.
Gideon's carrying tune.
Oren was up off the floor with the iron bar in his hand before the second drag. Lyra was past him. She did not remember getting past him. She had the canvas pulled back from the mouth of the arch, and the cold came in at her like a slap, and the snow, and the dark.
They were at the bottom of the Steps.
Three shapes in the falling snow, black against the gray ice of the river. The one in the middle hung between the other two with his arms over their shoulders and his head down. His left leg dragged behind him, straight as a post, the toe of the boot making a long groove in the snow on every step. The one on the left was small, with one arm in a sling and the other round the middle one's waist. The one on the right was tall and thin, in a gray coat, with no hat.
Lyra ran.
She did not mean to. She had told herself all evening that when he came back, if he came back, she would stand at the mouth of the arch with her arms folded and say something dry and cold, the way Hessa would, so that he would know she had not been afraid. Instead she ran down the slope of frozen mud and straw with her coat open and the Ledger clutched to her chest, and her boots went out from under her on the ice at the bottom, and she went down on one knee, hard, and got up again, and did not feel it.
"Here," said Gideon, in his flat small voice. "Take his arm. My good one's gone dead."
She took his arm.
It was the arm of an old man. Thin, in a ragged coat that smelled of lamp oil and soot. The hand that came down over her shoulder was in a black oily glove with the fingers worn through. And the face that came up, slowly, out of the dark, and looked at her from under the white wild eyebrows, was the face of a stranger. A broken nose. A small weak chin. Soot in every line. One eye half shut in a squint.
And under the left eye, the mole.
"You're late," said Lyra.
It came out the way she had planned. Dry. Cold. Like Hessa.
The stranger's mouth went down at the left corner.
"I know," said Corin. "I'm sorry." His voice was hoarse, and very tired, and it was his own. "There was a stair."
Oren was there then. He did not say anything. He gave the iron bar to Lyra without looking at her, and bent, and put one arm behind Corin's back and the other under his good knee, and lifted him up off the ice the way you lift a child who has fallen asleep in a chair. Corin made a sound through his teeth. The stiff leg stuck straight out in front of him, bound from hip to ankle in the gray strips of Hessa's mother's dress and the doctor's linen, and did not bend.
"Mind it," said Remy Castellan. "Mind the leg. It mustn't knock."
Oren looked at him over Corin's head. A long look. Then he turned, carefully, sideways, so that the stiff leg would not touch anything, and carried Corin up the slope and in under the canvas.
Lyra stood in the snow with the iron bar in one hand and the Ledger in the other.
Remy stood a little way off, at the foot of the Steps, with the snow coming down on his bare dark head. He had no hat. He had no gloves either. His hands were bare and white in the dark, and he was holding the left one in the right, the way you hold a hand that has been hurt. There was a fresh cut on the thumb. She could see the dark line of it.
"You'll come in," said Lyra. "To the fire."
"No." Remy shook his head. "I have to be back. Before the porters change at the first bell. If my bed is empty when Gant does his round—" He did not finish. He looked up the Steps, into the dark, toward the city. "I only came so far because he couldn't walk the last of it. Gideon couldn't carry him alone."
"Where's your hat?"
"I left it." Something moved in his face. "On a peg in Mrs. Pratt's coal store. With a lamp boy's ladder. If anybody asks, the lamp boy borrowed my hat to keep the snow off and took it with him." He paused. "Nobody will ask. Nobody asks about lamp boys."
"Gant will."
Remy looked at her.
"Yes," he said. "Gant will." He turned his hurt hand over and looked at the cut on the thumb, and closed his fingers over it. "Tell Mr. Vane that I'll send word. By the usual way. When I know what she's going to do with the box."
"What box?"
But he was already going. Up the Steps, two at a time, a thin gray shape in the snow, without a hat, without gloves, holding his own hand. And at the top he did not look back. He turned left, toward the bridges, and the dark took him.
Lyra went in.
Oren had laid Corin down on the pallet by the wall, on his back, with the stiff leg out straight on a folded blanket. Mother Grue was there already, leaning on her stick, looking down. Gideon was sitting on the floor at the foot of the pallet with his back to the brick and his eyes shut. His face was white. He was holding his bitten arm in its sling against his chest, and his lips were moving. Lyra could not hear the words. Then she understood that there were no words. He was humming. Without a sound.
Lyra put the Ledger down on the pallet, beside Corin's hand.
He put his hand on it at once. Flat. The way he always did. As if it were a dog that needed to know he was there.
"Tell me," she said.
Corin looked up at the curved black roof of the arch for a long time.
Then he told her.
He told her about the kitchen stair. The nine steps, and the turn, and the ninth one where his leg would not go. How he had sat there in the dark with the leg out across the step, and heard the voices coming down from above. A man's voice, pleasant, polite. And then hers.
"Elara," he said. "The Auditor. My sister." He said it the way you say a word in a language you are still learning. Carefully. Every sound. "She came down the stair, Lyra. With her clerks. And the big man, the one with the slate. And Gant behind them with a lantern." He swallowed. "And I couldn't move. I just sat there. On the step. With my leg across it like a bar. And she looked at me."
"Did she know you?"
"I don't know." He closed his eyes. "The big man picked me up. Lifted me down the steps. Like Oren did. Put me down at the bottom. And then he put his hand on my head." He opened his eyes again. "On my head, Lyra. Like you'd put a hand on a boy's head. And she said—" He stopped.
"What did she say?"
"Mind your leg, grandfather."
The brazier ticked.
Lyra did not say anything.
"And then she went into the counting room," said Corin, "and I went the other way. With Remy. Into the dark." His hand moved on the Ledger. "Through the iron door. It hums, Lyra. All the time. Like something breathing in its sleep. And it opened for Remy's hand, and it didn't like me, I could feel it not liking me, but it let me through because he was holding my wrist. And then the glass."
He stopped again.
He was quiet for so long that Lyra thought he had gone to sleep. His eyes were open. He was looking at nothing.
"Twelve steps," he said at last. "A passage of glass. Glass on both sides and over your head and under your feet, and something behind the glass, like a fog, and the fog looks at you. It reads you. All of you. All at once. Everything you've got left." His voice was very flat. "Remy said think about nothing. So I thought about nothing. I thought about the Ledger. The first page. I said it over and over in my head. Your name is Corin Vane. You are a harvester. You have a sister named Elara." He breathed out. "And it went through me like a hand through water. And came out the other side. And Remy said, Again. It has to know you. So we went back. And did it again. And the second time—"
He did not finish.
"The second time," said Lyra.
"The second time it was easier." Corin turned his head on the pallet and looked at her. "That's the bad part. It was easier. Like a dog that's smelled you once. It knows me now, Lyra. That thing in the glass knows me. Remy says that's what we needed. So that on Midwinter it'll open for me without him. It will know my face." His mouth moved. "I don't know if it'll let me forget it."
"And the jar? My father's—"
"Wasn't there." Corin shook his head on the pallet. "The shelf was empty. Remy had taken it up the back stair to the counting room, to be weighed. For the Bank. For her." He looked at the roof again. "She weighed it, Lyra. My sister. She put her hand on your father's last evening. Remy says she went white. Remy says she did something with a clause. Eleven. So that nobody can open it now unless the Fourth Desk is in the room." He laughed, very short, without any sound. "She's locked it. Against the Lady. Against us. Against everybody. Except herself."
Lyra sat down on the edge of the pallet.
"And then," said Corin, "on the way out. On the stair. My leg tore open again on the ninth step. I left blood on it. Quite a lot." He was quiet for a moment. "Gideon got me out through the coal store, and Remy caught us up in Cinder Lane, after. He'd been on that stair with her. After midnight. Lighting her way up with a lantern. And she stopped on the ninth step. And took off her glove. And touched it."
"Touched what?"
"My blood."
The word lay there between them.
"With her bare hand," said Corin. "Ledger-Sight. She read me, Lyra. Off the step. The way she read me in the autumn, through the glass, when our hands touched. And then she wiped it away with her glove, so that Gant wouldn't see it, and went out to her cab." He shut his eyes. "Whatever she saw, she saw it. And it cost her. It always costs her. Remy says she knelt on that step for a long time. And then she got up and went out into the snow and didn't look back."
Lyra looked down at his hand on the Ledger.
"Rule one," she said quietly.
Corin opened his eyes.
"Rule one," he said. "I wanted to stop. On the stair. When she said grandfather. I wanted to stand up and take my face off and say, It's me. It's Corin. You had braids." His hand closed on the Ledger. "And I didn't. I sat on the step with my leg out and let the big man carry me past her. And I didn't say anything." He looked at Lyra. "That's the truth. I was more afraid of her knowing than of her not knowing."
